title: Product (business) - Wikipedia
description:
For other uses, see [Product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(disambiguation)).

In **marketing and economics**, a **product** is any object, service, or system offered to a market to satisfy a [customer’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Customer) need or want. Products may be **tangible**, such as physical [goods](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goods) that can be touched and owned, or **intangible**, such as [services](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_(economics)), [digital currency products offerings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_product), or rights that provide value without physical form. Products are created through processes of design, production, and distribution, and they play a central role in [commercial exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commerce), consumer behavior, and organizational strategy.

Beyond marketing, the term _product_ is also used in fields such as **manufacturing**, where it refers to finished goods derived from raw materials, and **project management**, where it denotes deliverables produced to achieve defined objectives. [[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-:1-1) Because products directly affect consumer safety, economic activity, and environmental sustainability, they are often subject to **regulation, classification systems, and information-disclosure requirements** across different jurisdictions.

## Product classification
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/Eurail_Pass_and_Guide.jpg/250px-Eurail_Pass_and_Guide.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eurail_Pass_and_Guide.jpg) Eurail, a type of rail pass for multiple journeys by train, an intangible product

### By association
_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed)_] Companies such as [Pepsi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepsi) and [Coca-Cola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coca-Cola) are considered to have a very large and diverse product mix.

## Product model
For example, [Dyson Ltd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dyson_(company)), a manufacturer of appliances (mainly vacuum cleaners), requires customers to identify their model in the support section of the website.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-15) [Brand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brand) and model can be used together to identify products in the market. [[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-16)

Because of the huge amount of similar products in the [automotive industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automotive_industry), there is a special kind of defining a car with options (marks, attributes) that represent the characteristics of the vehicle. A model of a car is defined by some basic options like body, engine, gearbox, and axles. The variants of a model (often called the **trim levels**) are built with some additional options like color, seats, wheels, mirrors, other trims, entertainment, and assistant systems, etc. Options that exclude each other (pairwise) build an option family.

In addition, a specific unit of a product is often (and in some contexts must be) identified by a [serial number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serial_number), which is necessary to distinguish products with the same product definition.

## Product information
[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-23) Easily accessible and up-to-date medicinal product information can contribute to the [health literacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_literacy).

Production information-related developments can be useful for enabling, facilitating, or shifting towards [sustainable consumption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_consumption) and supporting more [sustainable productss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustainable_products). [[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-27) Consumers may seek reliable [information to evaluate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data-informed_decision-making) relevant characteristics of products such as durability and reliability. [[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Product_(business)#cite_note-29) The app CodeCheck gives some smartphone users some capability to scan products for assessed ingredients.

# Product definition: What is a product?
## Definition: What is a product?
A product is a tangible or intangible item that solves a need or delivers a desired outcome for a customer. It can be sold, licensed, or exchanged for value. Products may take many forms, including physical goods, software applications, services, or hybrids.

### Examples of products
Each of these offers a solution, benefit, or experience that someone is willing to pay for.

## Product characteristics and what customers look for
Size, shape, performance, price, and functionality — these are just a handful of attributes [customers](https://www.aha.io/roadmapping/guide/templates/customer-research) might consider before [purchasing](https://www.aha.io/roadmapping/guide/marketing-strategy/what-is-buyer-experience) your product.

## Different product types and audiences
### Consumer products
Consumer products, or business-to-consumer (B2C) products, are sold to end users and intended for personal use.

### Business products
These include raw materials, equipment, services, and software — [including SaaS tools](https://hbr.org/2023/04/the-rebirth-of-software-as-a-service) for project management, accounting, or customer support. Buying decisions often hinge on trial access, positive reviews, and clear pricing.

## What is the Complete Product Experience?
Definitionally, a product is an item or service to sell. But it is much more than that in reality. A product encompasses customers' entire experience with your company, from the moment they recognize a need to the [tools your team uses](https://www.aha.io/roadmapping/guide/product-management/which-tools-do-product-managers-use) to support them.

# What is a product? How to successfully build products users love
What is a product?

We all use the term “product” every day. But sometimes we mean different things. Let’s explore what a product really is.

A product is a solution crafted to solve a specific problem or fulfill its users’ needs. A product can be a physical, tangible object you can hold or a service you experience.

In this post, we’ll explore everything related to products.

## **Types of products**
You can touch and feel a **tangible product**, like your smartphone or sneakers. **Intangible products** are services or digital offerings. Think of streaming music services (Spotify, Apple Music) or cloud storage (Google Drive, Dropbox). Each has its quirks in development, marketing, and user experience.

We can categorize products further:

- Consumer goods – meant for personal use (groceries, clothing, etc)
- Industrial products – used to create other products (like machinery and raw materials)
- Services – encompass everything from haircuts to home cleaning
- Digital products – intangible goods that exist in digital form (software, digital media, etc)

Products are everywhere. And good products make our lives easier and more enjoyable. Not-so-great products can confuse or even irritate us. We want to focus on creating the first kind of course. We’ll also focus on intangible tech-related products in this article.

## **Product life cycle**
Understanding the PLC is crucial for product managers. It helps them plan, forecast, and manage a product’s journey effectively.

## **The complete product experience (CPE)**
It’s the full circle of interactions and experiences your users have with your product and brand.

This experience satisfies and retains customers.

## **Conclusion: products and effective product strategy**
A product is much more than just something you buy. It’s a solution to a problem, whether it’s something you can hold or a service you use.

The complete product experience ties it all together. It’s how users interact with your product from start to finish. Each part plays a role in making the experience as good as possible.

To build something valuable, keep your users’ needs at the center.

title: What is a Product? - Scrum.org
description:
# What is a Product?
0 from 0 ratings

Every great product starts with a simple idea: solving a problem in a way that matters to people and businesses alike. But what exactly defines a product—and what doesn’t?

“Winning products come from the deep understanding of the user’s needs combined with an equally deep understanding of what’s just now possible.” ― Marty Cagan, Inspired: How To Create Products Customers Love

## The Core Elements of a Product
A product is a solution that solves a meaningful problem for customers while driving measurable value for the business. It exists at the intersection of customer needs, business goals, and available technologies.

Successful products go beyond outputs—they are outcomes, delivering real impact by addressing specific problems in innovative and effective ways.

## Beyond Goods: How Services and Experiences Are Products, Too
A product isn’t limited to physical goods or digital tools—it also encompasses services. Services can be considered products when they deliver value and address customer needs through experiences or outcomes rather than tangible items.

Service-oriented solutions that behave like products:

Whether it’s a subscription-based model, a consulting offering, or an on-demand service, these solutions solve problems and create impact in much the same way as traditional products.

Like physical and digital products, services require thoughtful design, continuous iteration, and strategic alignment with customer and business objectives to succeed.

As we broaden the definition of products to include services, it’s also important to consider how products often combine elements to deliver even greater value.

## Composite Products: Building Solutions Through Integration
A product can be made up of other products. Many successful products are composites, integrating multiple components or services to deliver a cohesive solution. For instance, a smartphone combines hardware components like a screen, processor, and camera with software products like an operating system and apps to create a seamless user experience.

![composite products](https://scrumorg-website-prod.s3.amazonaws.com/drupal/inline-images/composite.png)

Similarly, service bundles or platforms often integrate various standalone offerings to provide greater value as a unified product. This modular approach enables flexibility, scalability, and the ability to adapt to evolving customer needs by leveraging existing products as building blocks.

## What Doesn’t Qualify as a Product? Defining the Boundaries
While many things can be considered products—physical goods, digital tools, services, or even experiences—something must deliver value, solve a problem, or meet a need to qualify as a product. Products are intentionally designed or curated to serve a specific purpose for a target audience.

For example, a raw material like timber isn’t inherently a product until it’s processed and positioned for a use, such as construction or furniture-making. Similarly, ideas, emotions, or abstract concepts are not products unless they are structured, packaged, and offered in a way that creates value for others—such as in art, media, or consulting services. Therefore, while many things have the potential to become products, the defining characteristic lies in their ability to deliver purposeful value.

## Final Thoughts
At its core, a product is about creating value—whether through goods, services, or experiences.
